measures.existing_conditions: The building’s HVAC systems operate using a mixture of local controls and a legacy building automation system (BAS) that provides limited monitoring capability. The control platform has not been comprehensively updated or recalibrated for several years, and the level of integration varies across equipment. Many components operate with minimal feedback, limited scheduling capability, and reduced visibility into equipment performance. Legacy or partially obsolete control devices are difficult to maintain, prone to failures, and may no longer be fully supported by the manufacturer.
measures.measure_title: Existing BAS Upgrade
measures.notes: Modernise the existing BAS and field devices onto an open digital platform with full feedback, trending and alarms to improve reliability, visibility and HVAC optimisation opportunities.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommends implementing a comprehensive BAS upgrade to provide modern, centralized control and monitoring of all major HVAC systems. The retrofit would consolidate the existing control infrastructure into a unified digital platform capable of advanced sequencing, optimized scheduling, remote monitoring, trending, and alarms. Outdated control devices would be replaced with new DDC components. A non-proprietary framework such as Niagara 4 is recommended to allow future expansion and easier maintenance. The upgraded BAS is expected to reduce energy use, improve comfort, and extend equipment service life. Enbridge Gas incentive programs for advanced building controls can help offset capital costs and improve project payback.

*Where applicable, IESO incentives and Enbridge incentives for central heating system efficiency upgrades may be available and could help improve overall project economics. Additional information regarding current incentive programs can be found on Mann Engineering’s website:

measures.existing_conditions:
The existing heating boilers in the mechanical room are non-condensing, gas-fired {______ }units installed in ______, with an estimated thermal efficiency of approximately _______%. As non-condensing equipment, they operate with higher flue-gas temperatures and cannot recover latent heat from combustion, resulting in reduced overall efficiency compared to modern condensing boiler technologies.

The boilers also not integrate with BAS, lack advanced control features such as setpoint adjustment based on outdoor air temperature and real-time modulation optimization. This limited control capability contributes to frequent short cycling and increased natural gas consumption. As a result, the system experiences elevated utility costs and higher greenhouse gas emissions.

While the boilers remain operational and continue to provide reliable heating performance, their age and conventional atmospheric design limit overall system efficiency compared to modern condensing technology. Although there is no immediate need for replacement, planning for a long-term boiler upgrade would allow the building to benefit from improved energy efficiency, reduced operating costs, and enhanced modulation and control capabilities in future years.
measures.measure_title: Condensing Boiler Retrofit
measures.notes: Replace aging non condensing boilers with high-efficiency condensing units and improved piping to enable true condensing operation, lowering gas consumption improve overall energy efficiency and extending plant life.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommended that the existing non-condensing boilers be replaced with high-efficiency condensing boilers. Condensing boilers are designed to extract additional heat from the flue gases by recovering latent heat through a secondary heat exchanger, allowing them to achieve thermal efficiencies of up to 98%. This upgrade would substantially reduce natural gas consumption, lower utility costs, and improve overall system performance.

Modern condensing boilers also provide advanced control capabilities, including high-turndown modulation, integrated sequencing, and seamless compatibility with Building Automation Systems (BAS). These features improve load matching, reduce equipment cycling, and enhance operational reliability.

Upgrading to condensing boiler technology not only increases energy efficiency and reduces ongoing operating costs but also supports long-term sustainability objectives and contributes to meaningful reductions in greenhouse gas emissions. Piping would be reconfigured to reduce standby losses and protect the boilers from thermal shock.

measures.existing_conditions:
The building currently operates with a traditional two-pipe fan coil system that provides either heating or cooling depending on the season. Each suite is equipped with an original fan coil unit that receives hot water from the central boiler plant during the heating season and chilled water from the central chiller and cooling tower during the cooling season.

Because the system is two-pipe, the fan coils cannot supply heating and cooling simultaneously. A full building changeover is required in the spring and fall to shift between heating and cooling modes. This limitation often results in periods of thermal discomfort during shoulder seasons, as individual suites have no ability to select heating or cooling independently.

The fan coils are original to the building and have surpassed their expected service life. Aging components, reduced reliability, and declining performance contribute to inconsistent temperature control, elevated maintenance requirements, and reduced energy efficiency
measures.measure_title: Water Source Heat Pump System Conversion
measures.notes: Replace seasonal fan-coil system with water-source heat pumps on a moderate-temperature loopallowing simultaneous heating and cooling and eliminating the central chiller.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann proposes the installation of a water source heat pump for winter and summer operation. The heat pump can be installed in the existing fan coil cabinet when the fan coils are scheduled for replacement. The existing piping can remain and be reused. The existing boiler plant can remain. The chiller is no longer required and only a fluid cooler can be installed in place of the existing cooling tower. This retrofit is ideal when the fan coils and chiller are scheduled for replacement as the incremental cost of the heat pump system compared to replacing the fan coils and chiller is marginal. The water source heat pump system is far more efficient than the existing fan coil system and is capable of heating or cooling operation at any time of the year. One consideration is the electrical supply in the suites as the heat pumps have a higher electrical demand compared to the fan coils since it consists of a compressor.

 As opposed to a 2-pipe fan coil system which operates at a design loop temp of 140F during heating season and 45F during cooling season, a water source heat pump system operates between 70-90F year around, meaning that the piping does not need to be insulated and there is minimal heat loss from the piping. It also means that the boiler system will always be operating in condensing temperatures with an extremely high thermal efficiency 95%+. Also, the heat input from the boiler system is greatly reduced meaning that the boiler plant can be downsized.

 In the heating season, the heat pumps extract heat from the hydronic loop and pump it into the suite. When more heat is required than is being generated within the building and most units are operating in heating mode, supplemental heating is supplied from a central boiler plant.

 In the cooling season, the heat pumps extract heat from the suites and pump it into the hydronic loop. When most of the units are in cooling mode and the heat is not needed elsewhere in the building, the heat is rejected from the loop using a fluid cooler. As opposed to a chiller, a fluid cooler comes at a much lower upfront and maintenance cost.

 During shoulder seasons, the system is capable of heat recycling, as heat from a suite calling for cooling such as a south elevation can transfer heat directly to another suite which is calling for heating such as a north elevation. In this case, no heat is rejected or input into the system.

 This measure eliminates the need for a chiller. Water source heat pump systems with fan coil units represent a sustainable and efficient HVAC solution suitable for a wide range of applications. By harnessing the thermal properties of water, these systems contribute to energy savings, environmental responsibility, and occupant comfort.

 *Further engineering details are required to finalize this measure..

measures.existing_conditions:
The building currently operates with separate upper-zone and lower-zone heating systems. The lower-zone system is served by a group of primary heating boilers supplying the lower-zone fan coil heating loop, make-up air (MUA) heating loop, and lower-zone domestic hot water (DHW) system through a heat exchanger.

The upper-zone system is arranged separately, with dedicated boilers serving the upper-zone fan coil and MUA heating loads, and separate boilers serving the upper-zone DHW system. This configuration increases the number of boilers required for upper-zone heating and DHW service and limits load-sharing flexibility between upper-zone space heating and DHW demands.
measures.measure_title: Upper-Zone Boiler and DHW Piping Reconfiguration to Primary–Secondary Arrangement
measures.notes: Reconfigure the upper-zone heating and DHW piping into a Primary–Secondary arrangement so the upper-zone heating boilers can also support DHW loads, reducing the need for dedicated DHW boilers and simplifying the boiler plant configuration.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
It is recommended to reconfigure the upper-zone heating and DHW system into a Primary–Secondary (P-S) hydronic arrangement. In the proposed design, the upper-zone boiler loop would circulate through the primary loop, while secondary loops would serve the upper-zone fan coil heating, MUA heating, and DHW heat exchanger loads. This would improve hydraulic separation and allow upper-zone space-heating and DHW loads to be served from a more coordinated boiler arrangement. With this redesign, the number of dedicated upper-zone DHW boilers may be reduced, subject to detailed engineering review.

measures.existing_conditions:
The Cooling tower is equipped with constant-speed or multi-speed fan motors that operate at discrete speeds regardless of the actual cooling load. Under part-load conditions, the fans still consume close to full power, resulting in unnecessary electrical usage and increased wear on mechanical components.
In addition, the condenser water pumps operate at constant speed, with no VFDs installed. As a result, pump output does not modulate with system demand, leading to unnecessary electrical energy consumption and increased mechanical wear during part-load operation.
measures.measure_title: VFD Retrofit for cooling tower fan and Condenser water pumps
measures.notes: Install VFDs on the cooling tower fan motors, suite circulation pumps, and condenser water pumps to enable demand-based modulation, reduce electrical energy consumption during part-load operation, lower noise and mechanical wear, and improve overall system efficiency and reliability.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
It is recommended to install variable frequency drives (VFDs) on the cooling tower fan motors. VFDs will allow fan speed to be modulated based on condenser water temperature, ambient conditions or BAS commands, so airflow more closely matches the required cooling load. Reducing fan speed yields large electrical savings due to the cubic relationship between power and speed, while also reducing noise and extending equipment life.
In addition, it is recommended to install variable frequency drives (VFDs) on the condenser water pump. The VFDs would allow pump speed to be modulated based on system demand, pressure, or temperature requirements, enabling flow rates to more closely match actual operating conditions. Reducing pump speed during part-load operation would result in meaningful electrical energy savings, reduced mechanical wear, and improved system reliability. Controls, sensors, and associated safeties would need to be updated and properly commissioned as part of this measure.

measures.existing_conditions: Corridor and common-area ventilation is provided by rooftop MUA units with constant-speed supply fans. These fans run at full speed whenever the units are enabled, independent of actual ventilation demand or occupancy. This results in higher electrical consumption and increased wear on motors and drive components.
measures.measure_title: MUA VFD Retrofit
measures.notes: Add VFDs to MUA supply fans with BAS integration so airflow tracks actual ventilation demand, cutting fan energy and mechanical wear while maintaining corridor pressure.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
It is recommended to retrofit the MUA supply fans with variable frequency drives (VFDs) and integrate them with the BAS. Fan speed would be reset based on duct static pressure, temperature, schedule, or occupancy. Under typical conditions, fan speed would be reduced during low-load periods while maintaining the ability to ramp up when higher ventilation rates are required. This measure reduces fan energy use, lowers mechanical stress, extends equipment life, and improves control of building pressurization and corridor comfort.

measures.existing_conditions: The {domestic hot water (DHW) system} and {make-up air (MUA) heating coils} are currently served by shell-and-tube heat exchangers connected to the primary heating loop. While these heat exchangers remain operational, shell-and-tube units typically require more space and are generally more difficult to service due to their construction. Maintenance activities such as inspection, descaling, and cleaning can be labor-intensive, which may limit long-term maintainability. In addition, shell-and-tube heat exchangers generally operate with lower heat transfer efficiency compared to modern plate-type heat exchangers.
measures.measure_title: Replace Shell-and-Tube Heat Exchangers with Plate-and-Frame Heat Exchangers {DHW and MUA Systems}
measures.notes: Replacing the existing shell-and-tube heat exchangers with modern plate-and-frame heat exchangers would improve heat transfer efficiency and significantly simplify long-term maintenance of systems.
measures.retrofit_conditions: It is recommended to replace the existing shell-and-tube heat exchangers serving the {DHW} and {MUA} systems with high-efficiency plate-and-frame heat exchangers. Plate-and-frame units provide higher heat transfer efficiency and allow closer temperature approaches between the primary and secondary loops. Their modular plate construction allows the exchanger to be easily opened for inspection, cleaning, and maintenance, significantly improving serviceability. This retrofit would improve overall heat transfer performance, simplify maintenance procedures, and enhance the long-term reliability and operational efficiency of both the DHW and ventilation heating systems.

measures.existing_conditions: Common areas and the garage are illuminated primarily by 4-ft T8 fluorescent fixtures and CFL spirals controlled by manual switches. These technologies have relatively high energy use and shorter lamp life compared to modern LED lighting.
measures.measure_title: Common Area and Garage Lighting Retrofit
measures.notes: Retrofit T8 and CFL lighting in common areas and garages to LED with occupancy/daylight controls to cut electricity use and maintenance while improving lighting quality.
measures.retrofit_conditions: Mann recommends retrofitting all existing T8 fluorescent fixtures and CFL spiral lamps with high-efficiency LED fixtures or lamps. LEDs consume significantly less electricity, have a longer lifespan, and reduce maintenance. Occupancy sensors or motion detectors should be installed in garages, mechanical rooms, laundry rooms, and other intermittently used spaces so lights operate only when needed. Daylight sensors can be added where natural light is available. This combined approach can substantially reduce electricity consumption, improve lighting quality and safety, and lower maintenance costs.

measures.existing_conditions: The building is equipped with double-pane windows typical of its construction era. The windows were observed to be in generally fair condition at the time of the site visit. However, in aging buildings, the insulating glazing units (IGUs) may gradually lose performance over time due to seal deterioration and potential reduction of the insulating gas between panes. While no widespread failure was observed, long-term thermal performance may decline as glazing systems age.
measures.measure_title: Window Lifecycle Planning and Sealant Renewal (Aging Double-Glazed Units)
measures.notes: Monitor aging double-pane windows and incorporate sealant renewal and long-term glazing upgrades into lifecycle and capital planning strategies.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
As part of ongoing building envelope maintenance and long-term capital planning, it is recommended to monitor window performance and implement periodic re-caulking and weatherstripping renewal where required. Full window replacement is not considered immediately necessary; however, future glazing upgrades should be evaluated in alignment with reserve fund studies and envelope lifecycle planning. Proactive lifecycle management will help maintain thermal performance, occupant comfort, and overall energy efficiency over time.

New glazing systems with improved low-E coatings, warm-edge spacers, and enhanced seal performance would significantly reduce heat loss, improve occupant comfort, and lower heating demand. Phased implementation can be considered to align with reserve fund planning and envelope lifecycle scheduling.

measures.existing_conditions: The building’s HVAC systems operate using a mixture of local controls and a legacy building automation system (BAS) that provides limited monitoring capability. The control platform has not been comprehensively updated or recalibrated for several years, and the level of integration varies across equipment. Many components operate with minimal feedback, limited scheduling capability, and reduced visibility into equipment performance. Legacy or partially obsolete control devices are difficult to maintain, prone to failures, and may no longer be fully supported by the manufacturer.
measures.measure_title: Existing BAS Upgrade
measures.notes: Modernise the existing BAS and field devices onto an open digital platform with full feedback, trending and alarms to improve reliability, visibility and HVAC optimisation opportunities.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommends implementing a comprehensive BAS upgrade to provide modern, centralized control and monitoring of all major HVAC systems. The retrofit would consolidate the existing control infrastructure into a unified digital platform capable of advanced sequencing, optimized scheduling, remote monitoring, trending, and alarms. Outdated control devices would be replaced with new DDC components. A non-proprietary framework such as Niagara 4 is recommended to allow future expansion and easier maintenance. The upgraded BAS is expected to reduce energy use, improve comfort, and extend equipment service life. Enbridge Gas incentive programs for advanced building controls can help offset capital costs and improve project payback.

*Where applicable, IESO incentives and Enbridge incentives for central heating system efficiency upgrades may be available and could help improve overall project economics. Additional information regarding current incentive programs can be found on Mann Engineering’s website:
https://www.mannengineering.com/100-000-enbridge-incentive

measures.existing_conditions:
The existing heating boilers in the mechanical room are non-condensing, gas-fired {______ }units installed in ______, with an estimated thermal efficiency of approximately _______%. As non-condensing equipment, they operate with higher flue-gas temperatures and cannot recover latent heat from combustion, resulting in reduced overall efficiency compared to modern condensing boiler technologies.

The boilers also not integrate with BAS, lack advanced control features such as setpoint adjustment based on outdoor air temperature and real-time modulation optimization. This limited control capability contributes to frequent short cycling and increased natural gas consumption. As a result, the system experiences elevated utility costs and higher greenhouse gas emissions.

While the boilers remain operational and continue to provide reliable heating performance, their age and conventional atmospheric design limit overall system efficiency compared to modern condensing technology. Although there is no immediate need for replacement, planning for a long-term boiler upgrade would allow the building to benefit from improved energy efficiency, reduced operating costs, and enhanced modulation and control capabilities in future years.
measures.measure_title: Condensing Boiler Retrofit
measures.notes: Replace aging non condensing boilers with high-efficiency condensing units and improved piping to enable true condensing operation, lowering gas consumption improve overall energy efficiency and extending plant life.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann recommended that the existing non-condensing boilers be replaced with high-efficiency condensing boilers. Condensing boilers are designed to extract additional heat from the flue gases by recovering latent heat through a secondary heat exchanger, allowing them to achieve thermal efficiencies of up to 98%. This upgrade would substantially reduce natural gas consumption, lower utility costs, and improve overall system performance.

Modern condensing boilers also provide advanced control capabilities, including high-turndown modulation, integrated sequencing, and seamless compatibility with Building Automation Systems (BAS). These features improve load matching, reduce equipment cycling, and enhance operational reliability.

Upgrading to condensing boiler technology not only increases energy efficiency and reduces ongoing operating costs but also supports long-term sustainability objectives and contributes to meaningful reductions in greenhouse gas emissions. Piping would be reconfigured to reduce standby losses and protect the boilers from thermal shock.

measures.existing_conditions:
The building currently operates with a traditional two-pipe fan coil system that provides either heating or cooling depending on the season. Each suite is equipped with an original fan coil unit that receives hot water from the central boiler plant during the heating season and chilled water from the central chiller and cooling tower during the cooling season.

Because the system is two-pipe, the fan coils cannot supply heating and cooling simultaneously. A full building changeover is required in the spring and fall to shift between heating and cooling modes. This limitation often results in periods of thermal discomfort during shoulder seasons, as individual suites have no ability to select heating or cooling independently.

The fan coils are original to the building and have surpassed their expected service life. Aging components, reduced reliability, and declining performance contribute to inconsistent temperature control, elevated maintenance requirements, and reduced energy efficiency
measures.measure_title: Water Source Heat Pump System Conversion
measures.notes: Replace seasonal fan-coil system with water-source heat pumps on a moderate-temperature loopallowing simultaneous heating and cooling and eliminating the central chiller.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
Mann proposes the installation of a water source heat pump for winter and summer operation. The heat pump can be installed in the existing fan coil cabinet when the fan coils are scheduled for replacement. The existing piping can remain and be reused. The existing boiler plant can remain. The chiller is no longer required and only a fluid cooler can be installed in place of the existing cooling tower. This retrofit is ideal when the fan coils and chiller are scheduled for replacement as the incremental cost of the heat pump system compared to replacing the fan coils and chiller is marginal. The water source heat pump system is far more efficient than the existing fan coil system and is capable of heating or cooling operation at any time of the year. One consideration is the electrical supply in the suites as the heat pumps have a higher electrical demand compared to the fan coils since it consists of a compressor.

 As opposed to a 2-pipe fan coil system which operates at a design loop temp of 140F during heating season and 45F during cooling season, a water source heat pump system operates between 70-90F year around, meaning that the piping does not need to be insulated and there is minimal heat loss from the piping. It also means that the boiler system will always be operating in condensing temperatures with an extremely high thermal efficiency 95%+. Also, the heat input from the boiler system is greatly reduced meaning that the boiler plant can be downsized.

 In the heating season, the heat pumps extract heat from the hydronic loop and pump it into the suite. When more heat is required than is being generated within the building and most units are operating in heating mode, supplemental heating is supplied from a central boiler plant.

 In the cooling season, the heat pumps extract heat from the suites and pump it into the hydronic loop. When most of the units are in cooling mode and the heat is not needed elsewhere in the building, the heat is rejected from the loop using a fluid cooler. As opposed to a chiller, a fluid cooler comes at a much lower upfront and maintenance cost.

 During shoulder seasons, the system is capable of heat recycling, as heat from a suite calling for cooling such as a south elevation can transfer heat directly to another suite which is calling for heating such as a north elevation. In this case, no heat is rejected or input into the system.

 This measure eliminates the need for a chiller. Water source heat pump systems with fan coil units represent a sustainable and efficient HVAC solution suitable for a wide range of applications. By harnessing the thermal properties of water, these systems contribute to energy savings, environmental responsibility, and occupant comfort.

 *Further engineering details are required to finalize this measure..

measures.existing_conditions:
The building currently operates with separate upper-zone and lower-zone heating systems. The lower-zone system is served by a group of primary heating boilers supplying the lower-zone fan coil heating loop, make-up air (MUA) heating loop, and lower-zone domestic hot water (DHW) system through a heat exchanger.

The upper-zone system is arranged separately, with dedicated boilers serving the upper-zone fan coil and MUA heating loads, and separate boilers serving the upper-zone DHW system. This configuration increases the number of boilers required for upper-zone heating and DHW service and limits load-sharing flexibility between upper-zone space heating and DHW demands.
measures.measure_title: Upper-Zone Boiler and DHW Piping Reconfiguration to Primary–Secondary Arrangement
measures.notes: Reconfigure the upper-zone heating and DHW piping into a Primary–Secondary arrangement so the upper-zone heating boilers can also support DHW loads, reducing the need for dedicated DHW boilers and simplifying the boiler plant configuration.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
It is recommended to reconfigure the upper-zone heating and DHW system into a Primary–Secondary (P-S) hydronic arrangement. In the proposed design, the upper-zone boiler loop would circulate through the primary loop, while secondary loops would serve the upper-zone fan coil heating, MUA heating, and DHW heat exchanger loads. This would improve hydraulic separation and allow upper-zone space-heating and DHW loads to be served from a more coordinated boiler arrangement. With this redesign, the number of dedicated upper-zone DHW boilers may be reduced, subject to detailed engineering review.

https://www.mannengineering.com/100-000-enbridge-incentive

measures.existing_conditions: No anti-scale thermostatic mixing valve was observed downstream of the domestic hot water storage tank during the site visit.As a result, delivery temperatures are controlled locally or through fixed settings, increasing the risk of temperature fluctuation, scalding, and scale buildup within downstream piping and fixtures.
measures.measure_title: Install Anti-Scale Thermostatic Mixing Valve
measures.notes: Install an anti-scale thermostatic mixing valve to improve DHW temperature control, enhance occupant safety, and reduce scaling-related maintenance.
measures.retrofit_conditions: Install an anti-scale thermostatic mixing valve on the domestic hot water system to maintain safe and stable delivery temperatures while protecting downstream piping and fixtures from scale buildup. This measure improves temperature control, reduces scald risk, and lowers long-term maintenance requirements by minimizing mineral scaling within the DHW system.

measures.existing_conditions:
The Cooling tower is equipped with constant-speed or multi-speed fan motors that operate at discrete speeds regardless of the actual cooling load. Under part-load conditions, the fans still consume close to full power, resulting in unnecessary electrical usage and increased wear on mechanical components.
In addition, the condenser water pumps operate at constant speed, with no VFDs installed. As a result, pump output does not modulate with system demand, leading to unnecessary electrical energy consumption and increased mechanical wear during part-load operation.
measures.measure_title: VFD Retrofit for cooling tower fan and Condenser water pumps
measures.notes: Install VFDs on the cooling tower fan motors, suite circulation pumps, and condenser water pumps to enable demand-based modulation, reduce electrical energy consumption during part-load operation, lower noise and mechanical wear, and improve overall system efficiency and reliability.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
It is recommended to install variable frequency drives (VFDs) on the cooling tower fan motors. VFDs will allow fan speed to be modulated based on condenser water temperature, ambient conditions or BAS commands, so airflow more closely matches the required cooling load. Reducing fan speed yields large electrical savings due to the cubic relationship between power and speed, while also reducing noise and extending equipment life.
In addition, it is recommended to install variable frequency drives (VFDs) on the condenser water pump. The VFDs would allow pump speed to be modulated based on system demand, pressure, or temperature requirements, enabling flow rates to more closely match actual operating conditions. Reducing pump speed during part-load operation would result in meaningful electrical energy savings, reduced mechanical wear, and improved system reliability. Controls, sensors, and associated safeties would need to be updated and properly commissioned as part of this measure.

measures.existing_conditions: Corridor and common-area ventilation is provided by rooftop MUA units with constant-speed supply fans. These fans run at full speed whenever the units are enabled, independent of actual ventilation demand or occupancy. This results in higher electrical consumption and increased wear on motors and drive components.
measures.measure_title: MUA VFD Retrofit
measures.notes: Add VFDs to MUA supply fans with BAS integration so airflow tracks actual ventilation demand, cutting fan energy and mechanical wear while maintaining corridor pressure.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
It is recommended to retrofit the MUA supply fans with variable frequency drives (VFDs) and integrate them with the BAS. Fan speed would be reset based on duct static pressure, temperature, schedule, or occupancy. Under typical conditions, fan speed would be reduced during low-load periods while maintaining the ability to ramp up when higher ventilation rates are required. This measure reduces fan energy use, lowers mechanical stress, extends equipment life, and improves control of building pressurization and corridor comfort.

measures.existing_conditions: The {domestic hot water (DHW) system} and {make-up air (MUA) heating coils} are currently served by shell-and-tube heat exchangers connected to the primary heating loop. While these heat exchangers remain operational, shell-and-tube units typically require more space and are generally more difficult to service due to their construction. Maintenance activities such as inspection, descaling, and cleaning can be labor-intensive, which may limit long-term maintainability. In addition, shell-and-tube heat exchangers generally operate with lower heat transfer efficiency compared to modern plate-type heat exchangers.
measures.measure_title: Replace Shell-and-Tube Heat Exchangers with Plate-and-Frame Heat Exchangers {DHW and MUA Systems}
measures.notes: Replacing the existing shell-and-tube heat exchangers with modern plate-and-frame heat exchangers would improve heat transfer efficiency and significantly simplify long-term maintenance of systems.
measures.retrofit_conditions: It is recommended to replace the existing shell-and-tube heat exchangers serving the {DHW} and {MUA} systems with high-efficiency plate-and-frame heat exchangers. Plate-and-frame units provide higher heat transfer efficiency and allow closer temperature approaches between the primary and secondary loops. Their modular plate construction allows the exchanger to be easily opened for inspection, cleaning, and maintenance, significantly improving serviceability. This retrofit would improve overall heat transfer performance, simplify maintenance procedures, and enhance the long-term reliability and operational efficiency of both the DHW and ventilation heating systems.

measures.existing_conditions: Common areas and the garage are illuminated primarily by 4-ft T8 fluorescent fixtures and CFL spirals controlled by manual switches. These technologies have relatively high energy use and shorter lamp life compared to modern LED lighting.
measures.measure_title: Common Area and Garage Lighting Retrofit
measures.notes: Retrofit T8 and CFL lighting in common areas and garages to LED with occupancy/daylight controls to cut electricity use and maintenance while improving lighting quality.
measures.retrofit_conditions: Mann recommends retrofitting all existing T8 fluorescent fixtures and CFL spiral lamps with high-efficiency LED fixtures or lamps. LEDs consume significantly less electricity, have a longer lifespan, and reduce maintenance. Occupancy sensors or motion detectors should be installed in garages, mechanical rooms, laundry rooms, and other intermittently used spaces so lights operate only when needed. Daylight sensors can be added where natural light is available. This combined approach can substantially reduce electricity consumption, improve lighting quality and safety, and lower maintenance costs.

measures.existing_conditions: The building is equipped with double-pane windows typical of its construction era. The windows were observed to be in generally fair condition at the time of the site visit. However, in aging buildings, the insulating glazing units (IGUs) may gradually lose performance over time due to seal deterioration and potential reduction of the insulating gas between panes. While no widespread failure was observed, long-term thermal performance may decline as glazing systems age.
measures.measure_title: Window Lifecycle Planning and Sealant Renewal (Aging Double-Glazed Units)
measures.notes: Monitor aging double-pane windows and incorporate sealant renewal and long-term glazing upgrades into lifecycle and capital planning strategies.
measures.retrofit_conditions:
As part of ongoing building envelope maintenance and long-term capital planning, it is recommended to monitor window performance and implement periodic re-caulking and weatherstripping renewal where required. Full window replacement is not considered immediately necessary; however, future glazing upgrades should be evaluated in alignment with reserve fund studies and envelope lifecycle planning. Proactive lifecycle management will help maintain thermal performance, occupant comfort, and overall energy efficiency over time.

New glazing systems with improved low-E coatings, warm-edge spacers, and enhanced seal performance would significantly reduce heat loss, improve occupant comfort, and lower heating demand. Phased implementation can be considered to align with reserve fund planning and envelope lifecycle scheduling.

Exhaust fans start and stop in response to measured CO levels, providing demand-based operation and reducing unnecessary runtime during periods of low vehicle activity. The garage fans and control system appeared to be functioning normally, with no obvious mechanical deficiencies reported.

The MUA systems were observed to be functionalwere originally installed circa 2004. Based on typical service life expectations for commercial ventilation equipment, the units are approaching the end of service life.
